newsitem.title: QATAR: ATHLETICS-IAAF DEFEND MEN-ONLY MEETING IN GULF STATE.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-IAAF DEFEND MEN-ONLY MEETING IN GULF STATE.

text.p: The world governing body of athletics has defended its decision to allow a men-only international meeting in this devoutly Moslem Gulf Arab state on Thursday.

"Whether or not women in some countries are allowed to take part alongside men is something which is entirely up to individual nations," said Hassan Ajabani, the International Amateur Athletic Federation's (IAAF) African representative.

"The IAAF has no plans to censure or dictate terms to countries where traditions don't allow women to take part in international competition...whether or not women are allowed to participate depends entirely on the organisers."
Qatar is assembling a bid for the 2006 Asian Games and may apply to host the 2001 world athletics championships.

"These are realistic bids," said Dahlan al-Hamad, head of the Qatar Athletic Federation. "The question of women taking part here will be overcome. By the time 2001 comes around, there will be a solution to these matters."
Hamad said in February, an exhibition table tennis match between two women professionals has been staged behind closed doors in front of an exclusively female audience.

He said also the Qatar Tennis and Squash Federation has had informal talks with the International Tennis Federation (ITF) about the possibility of a professional women's tennis tournament to be held in Doha.

The meeting will feature Olympic high jump champion Charles Austin, world 400 metres record holder Butch Reynolds, world high hurdles record holder Colin Jackson and former Olympic and world 100 metres champion Linford Christie.
Christie confirmed he would not compete at this year's world championships in Athens, saying he planned to compete for fun only now.
"I am through with big meets," Christie said. "Physically I am still strong but mentally I don't feel motivated enough. I am just out to enjoy myself."
